title: The Hardest Thing in Your Body
blurb: Enamel is harder than bone, your body only makes it once, and your teeth are quietly keeping a record of your whole life.

blocks.prompt: Read this out loud
blocks.text: Open your mouth and look in the mirror. Those white teeth are yours. Teeth help you bite an apple. Teeth help you chew your dinner. Your first teeth are called baby teeth. One day a tooth will feel wiggly. It will fall out. Then a bigger tooth grows in that spot. Brush your teeth every morning and every night. Keep them clean and strong.

blocks.prompt: Your Wiggly Tooth
blocks.text: Count your teeth with your tongue. You have about twenty. These are your baby teeth. They started growing before you were even born, hiding up inside your gums. Baby teeth do not stay forever. Under each one, a bigger tooth is waiting. When it is ready, it pushes up. The root of the baby tooth melts away. That is why the tooth goes wiggly. Then it falls out, and the grown-up tooth takes its place. You will grow thirty-two of those. They have to last the rest of your life, so brush them well.

3.title: The Hardest Thing in Your Body

notes: Four kinds: incisors, canines, premolars, molars
Incisors cut, molars grind
Enamel is the hardest thing your body makes
Elephant tusks are giant incisors
A narwhal tusk is one long spiral tooth

blocks.prompt: The Toolbox in Your Mouth
blocks.text: Run your tongue slowly across your teeth. They are not all the same shape, and that is not an accident. Each shape does a different job. At the front are your incisors. They are flat and sharp along the edge, like tiny shovels. Incisors slice. When you bite into a sandwich, your incisors do the cutting. Next to them sit your canines. These are the pointy ones. Canines grip and tear food that does not want to come apart, like a chewy piece of chicken. Behind those are the premolars and the molars. They are wide and bumpy on top, like little mountains. Their job is grinding. Your tongue pushes food onto them, your jaw closes, and they crush it into mush soft enough to swallow. So a single bite of an apple uses three different tools. The incisors cut the piece off, the canines hold it, and the molars grind it down. Your mouth is a whole toolbox, and you never have to think about it.

answers: they slice and cut food
the canines
so they can grind and crush food into mush
(inference: different foods need cutting, tearing, and grinding, so one shape could not do every job)

4.title: The Hardest Thing in Your Body
4.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 9 to 10
4.intro: Read the passage, then answer in full sentences. Some questions ask what you think, not just what the passage says.

meta.templateLabel: The Hardest Thing in Your Body

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Enamel is about 96 percent mineral
Enamel has no living cells, so it cannot heal
Plaque bacteria turn sugar into acid
Fluoride rebuilds enamel that acid struggles to dissolve
Saliva puts some mineral back
A cavity is the only hole your body never fills

blocks.prompt: The Thing Your Body Cannot Fix
blocks.text: Enamel is the hardest material your body makes. It is harder than your bones. It has to be, because it spends its whole life being smashed against other teeth, thousands of times a day, for decades. Enamel is nearly all mineral, packed into tight crystal rods standing side by side like a bundle of straws. There is a catch. Enamel is not alive. Bone is full of living cells that can rebuild a break. Enamel has none. The cells that built your enamel finished their work while the tooth was still buried in your jaw, and then they died. Whatever enamel you had the day your tooth came in is all the enamel you will ever get. So what wears it away? Not chewing. Bacteria. Your mouth is home to billions of them, and they gather in a sticky layer called plaque. Some of these bacteria love sugar as much as you do. When you eat something sweet, they eat too, and their waste is acid. That acid dissolves the mineral out of your enamel, atom by atom. Do that often enough and a soft spot opens, then a hole. That hole is a cavity, and your body cannot patch it. Saliva fights back. It washes acid away and carries calcium and phosphate that can put some mineral back, but only if it gets a quiet stretch of time to work. Fluoride helps too, by rebuilding enamel into a version that acid struggles to dissolve. Brushing is not really about food stuck in your teeth. It is about wrecking the plaque before the plaque wrecks the enamel.

answers: it is smashed against other teeth thousands of times a day for decades
the cells that built it died when the tooth came in, so nothing is left to rebuild it
wrecking the plaque before the plaque wrecks the enamel
(inference: saliva needs a quiet stretch of time to put mineral back, and constant snacking never gives it any)

5.title: The Hardest Thing in Your Body
5.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for ages 11 to 12
5.intro: Read the passage, then answer in full sentences. Use evidence from the text where the question asks for it.

meta.templateLabel: The Hardest Thing in Your Body

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Enamel grows in layers like tree rings
The neonatal line marks the day you were born
Hardened plaque is called calculus
Calculus traps pollen, starch, and even paint
Teeth outlast every other part of a body
Lapis lazuli in one woman's teeth rewrote who painted medieval books

blocks.prompt: The Diary in Your Mouth
blocks.text: Your teeth are keeping a diary, and you did not agree to it. Enamel is laid down in layers, a little at a time, the way a tree adds rings. Under a microscope those layers show up as fine lines running through the tooth. Some mark a single day of growth. Others mark roughly a week. Count them and you can work out how old a tooth was, almost to the day, when it stopped growing. One line stands out from all the others. Every baby tooth carries a dark band called the neonatal line. It marks the moment you were born. Growing a tooth inside a warm, quiet womb is one thing; growing it in the outside world is another, and the change is severe enough that the enamel records the jolt. You are carrying the timestamp of your own birth around in your mouth. The diary goes further. If you were sick as a young child, or badly short of food, your enamel may hold a groove where growth faltered. Those grooves do not fade. Archaeologists dig up people who died a thousand years ago and read the hard years straight off their teeth. Even the gunk helps. Plaque that is never brushed off hardens into a rocky crust called calculus, and calculus traps whatever was floating past: pollen, starch grains, bits of the food a person ate. In 2019 researchers examined the teeth of a woman buried at a German monastery around the year 1100 and found brilliant blue flecks of lapis lazuli, a precious stone ground into paint and hauled across the world from Afghanistan. She had been licking her brush to sharpen the point. Her teeth proved that medieval women, not only monks, painted the great illuminated books. No one wrote her name down. Her teeth told on her anyway.

6.title: The Hardest Thing in Your Body
6.subtitle: A reading and science sheet for age 13
6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

meta.templateLabel: The Hardest Thing in Your Body

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Enamel: about 96 percent mineral, the hardest tissue in the body
Ameloblasts build enamel, then die at eruption
Dentin can thicken for life; enamel cannot
Streptococcus mutans turns sugar into enamel-dissolving acid
Wisdom teeth are third molars, often with no room left
Teeth survive tens of thousands of years in the ground

blocks.prompt: The One Material Your Body Only Makes Once
blocks.text: Almost everything in your body is under repair. Break a bone and cells swarm the fracture, lay down new tissue, and knit it back so completely that the seam can become as strong as the bone around it. Cut your skin and it closes. Damage your liver and it regrows. Your body is, by default, a construction site that never shuts down. Enamel is the exception. It is the hardest substance your body produces, roughly ninety-six percent mineral by weight, harder than bone, built from crystal rods packed so tightly that they can survive a lifetime of being hammered against other crystal rods thousands of times a day. And your body will never make another speck of it. The reason is a decision made before you were born. Enamel is built by cells called ameloblasts. They work from inside the jaw, laying the enamel down over months, and when the tooth finally pushes through the gum, the ameloblasts are finished. They do not retire to some reserve. They die, and they are shed. The tooth erupts into your mouth carrying every atom of enamel it will ever have. Dentin, the softer layer underneath, keeps its builder cells and can thicken slowly over the years. Enamel gets nothing. A chip is permanent. A cavity is permanent. A dentist does not heal a tooth; a dentist cleans out the ruin and fills the space with something manufactured. This looks like a design flaw, and for most of human history it was not. Enamel is expensive: it demands enormous amounts of mineral and a long build. Evolution weighs cost against need, and for millions of years the need was modest. Hunted meat, wild plants, tubers, and the occasional wild fruit are tough and abrasive but almost never sugary. The bacteria that hollow out teeth, Streptococcus mutans chief among them, need fermentable sugar to make the acid that dissolves mineral. Give them almost none and a set of unrepairable enamel is a perfectly good bet. It only needs to last as long as you do. Then we changed the terms. Farming brought grain. Trade brought refined sugar. Now we drink it. Untreated tooth decay is one of the most widespread health conditions on the planet, not because our teeth got worse, but because we started feeding the bacteria on a schedule our enamel was never designed to survive. The jaw tells the same story from a different angle. Our diets grew soft and processed, and the human jaw grew shorter over the same span, but the tooth count did not follow. Thirty-two teeth still try to fit. The last four, the third molars we call wisdom teeth, arrive around age eighteen to find no room, and millions of people have them cut out. There is one consolation. Because enamel is inert and nearly indestructible, it outlasts everything else we are made of. Skin, muscle, and eventually bone all surrender. Teeth do not. They sit in the ground for tens of thousands of years holding their growth lines, their birth mark, their record of hungry seasons, and the hardened plaque with a person's last meals sealed inside. The one part of you that your body refuses to repair is the one part most likely to still be here long after the rest of you is gone.
